Lab 03.1 — Linear Regression with the Kaggle House Prices Dataset¶

Course: Data Analysis with Python — Data Science Linear Regression Lab Dataset: House Prices – Advanced Regression Techniques (Kaggle), train.csv — 1,460 homes sold in Ames, Iowa (2006–2010) Target variable: SalePrice (USD)

Contents¶

Section Content
Step 1 Data preparation: load, inspect, missing-value audit and imputation strategy
Step 2 Exploratory data analysis: scatter plots and Pearson/Spearman correlations
Step 3 Build the linear regression model (80/20 split), intercept and coefficients
Step 4 Evaluate: MSE, RMSE, MAE, R², actual-vs-predicted and residual diagnostics
Step 5 Extension: more features, standardisation, interaction terms, multicollinearity (VIF)
Report Strengths, limitations and consolidated answers to every discussion question

Every Discussion Questions block from the lab sheet is answered in a markdown cell immediately after the code that produces the evidence for it.

Step 0 — Setup¶

Imports and a single shared plotting style, so every figure in the report is consistent: one accessible colour per series, recessive grid and axes, thin marks. Figures are also written to figures/ as PNGs for reuse in slides.

Missing-data strategy¶

Reading data_description.txt is essential here: for most of these columns NA is not an unrecorded value — it is a documented category meaning the feature does not exist (PoolQC = "NA: No Pool", Alley = "No alley access", BsmtQual = "No Basement", GarageType = "No Garage", FireplaceQu = "No Fireplace"). Deleting those rows would throw away 1,453 houses simply for not having a pool. The strategy therefore splits into four rules:

Rule Columns Action Reason
1. Structural NA → explicit category PoolQC, MiscFeature, Alley, Fence, FireplaceQu, Garage*, Bsmt*, MasVnrType fill with the string "None" NA means "feature absent" — that is information, not a gap
2. Numeric counterpart of an absent feature GarageYrBlt, MasVnrArea fill with 0 no garage ⇒ no garage year; no veneer ⇒ 0 ft²
3. Genuinely unknown numeric LotFrontage (17.7%) median within Neighborhood frontage is driven by the street layout, so neighbourhood peers are the best estimate; the median resists the right skew
4. Genuinely unknown categorical Electrical (1 row) mode of the column a single row; the mode (SBrkr) is the safe fill

Why not just drop? Dropping rows with any NA leaves 0 usable rows (every house is missing at least one of PoolQC/Alley/Fence); dropping the 19 columns would discard useful predictors such as LotFrontage and FireplaceQu. Imputation preserves all 1,460 observations.

One point worth stressing for the modelling that follows: the four features used in Steps 2–4 (GrLivArea, OverallQual, YearBuilt, GarageArea) and the target SalePrice have no missing values at all, so the regression results do not depend on any imputation choice. The cleaning below makes the full table usable and keeps the pipeline honest for the extension in Step 5.

In [6]:
df = df_raw.copy()

# Rule 1 - "NA" is a real category meaning the feature is absent
none_cols = ["PoolQC", "MiscFeature", "Alley", "Fence", "FireplaceQu", "MasVnrType",
             "GarageType", "GarageFinish", "GarageQual", "GarageCond",
             "BsmtQual", "BsmtCond", "BsmtExposure", "BsmtFinType1", "BsmtFinType2"]
df[none_cols] = df[none_cols].fillna("None")

# Rule 2 - numeric counterpart of an absent feature
df[["GarageYrBlt", "MasVnrArea"]] = df[["GarageYrBlt", "MasVnrArea"]].fillna(0)

# Rule 3 - LotFrontage: median within the neighbourhood
df["LotFrontage"] = df.groupby("Neighborhood")["LotFrontage"].transform(
    lambda s: s.fillna(s.median()))
df["LotFrontage"] = df["LotFrontage"].fillna(df["LotFrontage"].median())  # safety net

# Rule 4 - single unknown categorical
df["Electrical"] = df["Electrical"].fillna(df["Electrical"].mode()[0])

print(f"Missing values remaining: {df.isna().sum().sum()}")
print(f"Rows kept: {len(df):,} of {len(df_raw):,}  ({len(df)/len(df_raw)*100:.0f}% - nothing dropped)")
print("\nSanity check - rows that would survive a naive dropna():",
      len(df_raw.dropna()))

Discussion questions — Step 1¶

Q1. How many columns have missing values? 19 of the 81 columns (23.5%), accounting for 7,829 missing cells — 6.62% of all cells in the table. Five columns are missing in more than half their rows: PoolQC (99.5%), MiscFeature (96.3%), Alley (93.8%), Fence (80.8%) and MasVnrType (59.7%). At the other end, Electrical is missing in a single row. The five Garage* columns are missing in exactly the same 81 rows, and the five Bsmt* columns in the same ~37 rows — a strong hint that the missingness is structural rather than random.

Q2. What strategy did you choose to handle missing data, and why? A category-aware imputation rather than deletion, in the four rules tabulated above: "None" for absent-feature categoricals, 0 for their numeric counterparts, neighbourhood median for LotFrontage, column mode for Electrical. The reasoning:

  1. The missingness is informative, not random. data_description.txt documents NA as a level ("No Pool", "No Garage"). Treating it as a gap destroys a real signal: having no basement is a genuine, price-relevant fact.
  2. Deletion is not available. dropna() on rows returns 0 rows; dropping the 19 columns loses real predictors. Imputation keeps all 1,460 houses.
  3. Grouped median for LotFrontage. It is the only sizeable column where NA really means "unknown". Lot frontage is determined by street and block layout, so the Neighborhood median is a much better estimate than a global mean, and the median is robust to the long right tail of lot sizes.
  4. No leakage. Every fill uses predictor information only — never SalePrice.

Step 2 — Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Tasks: select 3–4 numerical features likely related to SalePrice, plot each against the target, and compute the Pearson correlations.

The four features and why they were chosen¶

Feature Meaning (data_description.txt) Why it should drive price
GrLivArea Above-grade living area, ft² Size is the headline number in any listing; price per ft² is how the market quotes value
OverallQual Overall material & finish quality, ordinal 1–10 Captures finish level and condition, which size alone cannot
YearBuilt Original construction year Proxy for age, layout fashion, insulation, wiring and remaining service life
GarageArea Garage size, ft² A priced amenity in Iowa's climate and a proxy for the overall scale of the property

OverallQual is an ordinal integer, not a continuous measurement. Treating it as numeric — as the lab asks — assumes the steps 1→2 and 9→10 are worth the same amount of money. That assumption is imperfect (the real pattern is convex) and is examined with an interaction term in Step 5.

# ---- Pearson (linear) and Spearman (monotonic) correlations --------------
rows = []
for feat in FEATURES:
    r, p   = stats.pearsonr(df[feat], df[TARGET])
    rs, ps = stats.spearmanr(df[feat], df[TARGET])
    rows.append({"feature": feat, "pearson_r": round(r, 4), "p_value": f"{p:.2e}",
                 "r_squared_alone": round(r**2, 4), "spearman_rho": round(rs, 4),
                 "gap_rho_minus_r": round(rs - r, 4),

Discussion questions — Step 2¶

Q1. Which variable has the strongest correlation with SalePrice? Is it positive or negative?

OverallQual, with Pearson r = 0.791 — positive (p ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻³¹³, i.e. indistinguishable from zero probability of arising by chance). On its own it explains r² = 62.6% of the variance in price. The full ranking is:

Rank Feature Pearson r Direction Variance explained alone
1 OverallQual 0.791 positive 62.6%
2 GrLivArea 0.709 positive 50.2%
3 GarageArea 0.623 positive 38.9%
4 YearBuilt 0.523 positive 27.3%

All four are positive, which matches intuition: better finish, more living space, a bigger garage and a newer build all raise the price. None of the four is negatively correlated with the target.

Q2. Do you see any signs of non-linear relationships?

Yes — three distinct signs:

  1. Spearman ρ exceeds Pearson r for every feature, and most sharply for YearBuilt (ρ = 0.653 vs r = 0.523, a gap of +0.130). Spearman only asks whether the relationship is monotonic; Pearson asks whether it is a straight line. The gap is the signature of a monotonic but curved relationship — mean price is roughly flat (even dipping) for houses built before 1950 and then climbs steeply, from $148k for 1950–1970 builds to $245k for post-2000 builds.
  2. The quality ladder is convex (panel a). Going from quality 5 to 6 adds about $28k to the mean price, whereas 8 to 9 adds about $93k. A single linear coefficient on OverallQual must average these very unequal steps, so it over-prices the bottom of the ladder and under-prices the top.
  3. The variance is not constant (panel b). The price scatter around the trend widens steadily with size: within 0–1000 ft² the standard deviation of price is ≈ $26k, but above 2200 ft² it is ≈ $121k — a 4.6× increase. That "fan" shape is heteroscedasticity — it violates the constant-variance assumption of OLS, and it is why the model's dollar errors are largest for expensive houses (shown in Step 4). Taking logs of the target (panel c) largely removes it: skewness falls from 1.88 to 0.12, and the log model is tested in Step 5.

Two further caveats visible in the plots: the four houses above 4,000 ft² are leverage points — two of them (Id 524 and 1299, SaleCondition = Partial, unfinished sales of quality-10 homes) sold for far below what their size implies and distort any straight line; and GarageArea = 0 for 81 houses (no garage), which puts a spike of points on the y-axis that a linear term fits poorly.

Step 3 — Build the Linear Regression Model¶

Tasks: split the data 80/20, train a linear regression on the selected features, and display the intercept and coefficients.

The fitted regression equation¶

predicted SalePrice = -845,603.74
                    +      52.97  x  GrLivArea     (ft2 of above-grade living area)
                    +  22,708.55  x  OverallQual   (quality points, 1-10)
                    +     395.57  x  YearBuilt     (construction year)
                    +      57.70  x  GarageArea    (ft2 of garage)

In words: a house's predicted price starts from a (non-interpretable) baseline of −$845,604 and adds $52.97 for every square foot of above-grade living area, $22,708.55 for every one-point gain in overall quality, $395.57 for every year newer it was built, and $57.70 for every square foot of garage.

Discussion questions — Step 3¶

Q1. Write down the regression equation you obtained.

predicted SalePrice = -845,603.74 + 52.97 x GrLivArea + 22,708.55 x OverallQual
                                  + 395.57 x YearBuilt + 57.70 x GarageArea

A note on the intercept: −$845,604 is the predicted price of a house with 0 ft² of living area, quality 0, built in year 0 and with no garage — a combination that cannot exist. It is a mathematical anchor that lets the plane pass through the data cloud (which sits at YearBuilt ≈ 1971, where the YearBuilt term alone contributes ≈ +$780k), not a meaningful price. This is why the standardised version in Step 5, whose intercept equals the mean price, is easier to read.

Q2. How much does SalePrice increase/decrease for one unit change in GrLivArea?

It increases by $52.97 per additional square foot, holding quality, year built and garage area constant. Equivalently:

  • +$5,297 per extra 100 ft² of living space;
  • ≈ +$27,778 for one standard deviation of living area (524 ft²).

Two qualifications matter. First, the simple regression of price on GrLivArea alone gives a slope of about $102/ft² — nearly twice as steep (R² = 0.484 on its own). The multiple-regression coefficient is smaller because big houses also tend to be higher quality (r = 0.59 between GrLivArea and OverallQual), so part of what raw size appeared to buy is really quality, and the model now credits it to OverallQual. Second, this is an associational statement under a linear, constant-effect assumption, not proof that adding 100 ft² to your own house would raise its sale price by exactly $5,297.

Q3. Are there any features with negative coefficients? What do they imply?

No — all four coefficients are positive (52.97, 22,708.55, 395.57, 57.70), so each feature pushes the prediction up, matching the positive correlations found in Step 2. The only negative number in the model is the intercept, which is not a feature effect.

Had a coefficient come out negative, it would mean one of three things:

  1. A genuine negative effect — e.g. OverallCond can be negative in some specifications because a high "condition" score often marks an old house that has been patched up rather than a desirable new one.
  2. A suppression / collinearity artefact — with correlated predictors, a feature's sign can flip once another absorbs the shared signal. If TotalBsmtSF and 1stFlrSF (r ≈ 0.82) both enter a model, one frequently turns negative even though both raise price on their own. The honest reading is then "conditional on the other, this adds nothing", not "this lowers price".
  3. A sign of mis-specified form — forcing a straight line on a curved relationship can produce a negative term that is really doing curvature repair.

This is worth watching in Step 5: the interaction model drives GrLivArea's own coefficient from $46.07 down to $1.26/ft² — close to flipping negative — purely because the interaction term takes over the size effect.

Discussion questions — Step 4¶

Q1. What is the R² value? What does it indicate about your model's performance?

R² = 0.7695 on the held-out test set (0.7454 on the training set; 5-fold cross-validated R² = 0.7362 ± 0.1027). The accompanying errors are MSE = 1,767,706,248, i.e. RMSE = $42,044 and MAE = $26,879 (MAPE = 16.2%, and RMSE is 23.5% of the mean test price).

What it means:

  • 76.95% of the variance in sale price is explained by just four features; the remaining 23% is down to everything the model cannot see — neighbourhood, lot shape, basement finish, kitchen quality, market timing — plus genuine noise in how individual sales are negotiated.
  • Test R² ≥ train R² (0.7695 vs 0.7454), so the model is not overfitting. The cross-validated folds do vary (0.53 to 0.80): the weak fold is the one that happens to contain several of the extreme luxury houses, which is itself evidence of how much the tail of the price distribution drives the score — any single train/test split of this dataset should be read with that sensitivity in mind. With four parameters and 1,168 training rows that is expected; if anything the model is slightly under-fit (high bias), which is the normal price of a simple linear specification.
  • In practical terms the accuracy is moderate, not production-grade. A typical prediction is off by about $27k (MAE) on a mean price of $182k — roughly 15%. That is useful for a rough automated valuation or a sanity check on an asking price, but far too loose to settle a transaction. The headroom is large: this model uses 4 of the 79 available predictors and assumes a straight line, whereas the full-feature gradient-boosted models that top the Kaggle leaderboard for this dataset cut the error substantially further.
  • R² alone would hide the structure of the errors. The residual plot shows the errors are heteroscedastic and strongly right-skewed (skew = 2.94), so the single R² number overstates how trustworthy the model is for any individual expensive house.

Q2. In which price range (low/high) does the model perform poorly?

Both ends fail, but in opposite ways — which is why the two panels above use different measures:

Quartile Price range n Mean error (signed) RMSE MAPE
Q1 lowest ≤ $127,000 75 +$3,667 (over-predicts) $28,467 25.1%
Q2 $127k–154k 71 +$304 $24,962 14.1%
Q3 $154k–209k 73 +$11,842 $26,307 12.3%
Q4 highest > $209,175 73 −$29,665 (under-predicts) $70,286 12.8%
  • In dollar terms the model is worst on expensive houses. The top quartile's RMSE ($70,286) is 2.6× the average of the other three quartiles ($25–28k), and the error is systematically negative: the model under-prices the top quartile by $29,665 on average. All five of the largest misses are luxury homes, led by a $755,000 house predicted at $446,856 (−$308,144, a 41% shortfall). The cause is structural: a straight line cannot reproduce the convex quality ladder of Step 2, and the premium features of a luxury home (pool, 3-car garage, premium neighbourhood, superb kitchen) are simply absent from the four features.
  • In percentage terms the model is worst on cheap houses. The bottom quartile carries a MAPE of 25.1% — double the middle of the market — and a slight upward bias. The floor of the straight line is too high for small, old, low-quality houses: with four positive coefficients the model has no way to predict a price below a certain level, so the cheapest homes get pulled up toward the mean.
  • The middle of the market ($127k–$209k) is where the model is reliable: near-zero bias in Q2 and 12–14% relative error. That is also where the bulk of the data sits, so OLS — which minimises squared error — optimises for exactly this region and tolerates the tails.

Step 5 — Extension¶

All three suggested extensions are carried out and compared against the Step 3 baseline on the same 80/20 split, so every R² below is measured on the same 292 held-out houses:

  1. More features — add TotalBsmtSF and LotArea (GarageArea is already in).
  2. Standardisation — z-score the predictors and re-read the coefficients.
  3. Interaction term — GrLivArea × OverallQual.

Plus a fourth, motivated by the non-linearity found in Step 2: modelling log(SalePrice) instead of the raw price. Multicollinearity is then measured with variance inflation factors.

5.5 — Multicollinearity¶

In [28]:
def vif_table(frame):
    # Variance inflation factor: VIF_j = 1 / (1 - R2_j), where R2_j comes from
    # regressing feature j on all the other features.
    out = {}
    for col in frame.columns:
        others = frame.drop(columns=[col])
        r2_j = LinearRegression().fit(others, frame[col]).score(others, frame[col])
        out[col] = 1 / (1 - r2_j)
    return pd.Series(out, name="VIF").round(2)

Xi_all = df[EXTENDED].copy()
Xi_all["GrLivArea_x_OverallQual"] = Xi_all["GrLivArea"] * Xi_all["OverallQual"]

# Centring the two parent features before multiplying them
Xc_all = df[EXTENDED].copy()
Xc_all["GrLivArea_x_OverallQual_centred"] = (
    (df["GrLivArea"] - df["GrLivArea"].mean()) * (df["OverallQual"] - df["OverallQual"].mean()))

vifs = pd.concat([
    vif_table(df[FEATURES]).rename("baseline (4 feats)"),
    vif_table(df[EXTENDED]).rename("extended (6 feats)"),
    vif_table(Xi_all).rename("with raw interaction"),
    vif_table(Xc_all).rename("with centred interaction"),
], axis=1)
print("Variance inflation factors  (rule of thumb: >5 is a concern, >10 is severe)\n")

Discussion questions — Step 5¶

Q1. Does adding more features improve the model?

Yes, but with sharply diminishing returns, and the form of the model matters more than the number of features. On the identical test set:

Model Features Test R² ΔR² Test RMSE
1. Baseline (Step 3) 4 0.7695 — $42,044
2. + TotalBsmtSF, LotArea 6 0.7957 +0.0262 $39,584
3. Standardised 6 0.7957 +0.0262 $39,584
4. + GrLivArea × OverallQual 7 0.8239 +0.0544 $36,752
5. log(SalePrice), 6 features 6 0.8642 +0.0947 $32,269

Reading the table:

  • Two extra features buy +2.6 points of R² and cut RMSE by $2,460. TotalBsmtSF earns its place (standardised effect ≈ $8,576 per SD); LotArea is the weakest of the six (≈ $6,970 per SD, simple r = 0.26 — in Ames the land is cheap relative to the structure on it).
  • The single interaction term adds more than the two extra features did (+0.028 on top of model 2), confirming the convexity seen in Step 2: a square foot in a quality-10 house is worth far more than a square foot in a quality-4 house. The fitted marginal value of a square foot runs from ≈ $28/ft² at quality 4 to ≈ $68/ft² at quality 10.
  • Fixing the target distribution beats adding features. Simply regressing log(SalePrice) on the same six predictors gives the largest gain of all (R² = 0.8642, RMSE $32,269, MAE $20,303) because it matches the multiplicative reality of house prices and tames the heteroscedasticity diagnosed in Step 2. It also improves the weak spots found in Step 4: MAPE on the cheapest quartile falls from 25.1% to 19.6%, overall MAPE from 16.2% to 12.3%, and the top-quartile RMSE from $70,286 to $54,807.
  • Standardisation changes nothing about fit — R² is identical to six decimal places, as it must be, since a linear rescaling of the predictors is absorbed by the coefficients. What it changes is readability: the intercept becomes the mean training price ($181,441.54) and the coefficients become comparable "USD per standard deviation" effects, which rank the drivers OverallQual ($29,879) > GrLivArea ($24,150) > YearBuilt ($11,181) > GarageArea ($9,531) > TotalBsmtSF ($8,576) > LotArea ($6,970). On the raw scale OverallQual's coefficient of 21,856 looks ~470× larger than GrLivArea's 46.07, but that is an artefact of one being a 1–10 scale and the other square feet — on a common footing the two are close, with quality just ahead.
  • R² must not be the only criterion. R² never falls when a feature is added, so "more is better" is guaranteed on the training set and must be checked on held-out data (as above). Here the test score rises too, so the gains are real rather than overfitting — with 1,168 rows and 7 parameters there is plenty of data per parameter.

Q2. Are there any signs of multicollinearity in your model?

Mild and harmless in the feature-only models; severe — but artificial — once the raw interaction term is added.

Feature Baseline (4) Extended (6) + raw interaction + centred interaction
GrLivArea 1.74 1.86 15.98 1.97
OverallQual 2.40 2.52 7.16 2.53
YearBuilt 1.70 1.72 1.73 1.73
GarageArea 1.66 1.74 1.74 1.74
TotalBsmtSF — 1.63 1.67 1.67
LotArea — 1.13 1.13 1.13
interaction — — 30.59 1.19
  • Models 1–3 are clean. Every VIF is below 2.6, far under the usual thresholds (>5 a concern, >10 severe), and no pairwise correlation among the six predictors exceeds 0.593 (GrLivArea–OverallQual). The coefficients are therefore stable and safe to interpret. There is visible redundancy — OverallQual correlates 0.57 with YearBuilt and 0.56 with GarageArea, because newer houses are built to higher standards and with bigger garages — and it is exactly this overlap that shrinks GrLivArea's slope from $102 to $53/ft² between the simple and multiple regressions. But it is not severe enough to destabilise the fit.
  • Model 4 shows textbook structural multicollinearity. GrLivArea × OverallQual is by construction almost a linear function of its parents, so its VIF hits 30.6 and GrLivArea's jumps to 16.0. The symptom is visible in the coefficients: GrLivArea collapses from $46.07 to $1.26/ft² and OverallQual from $21,856 to $12,059 — the parent terms have become uninterpretable on their own even though the model as a whole predicts better.
  • The fix is centring, and it is free. Multiplying the mean-centred parents instead gives the identical test R² of 0.8239 while every VIF drops back below 2.6 (interaction: 1.19). This is the key lesson about multicollinearity: it inflates the standard errors and instability of individual coefficients, not the model's predictive accuracy. If the goal is interpretation, centre the interaction (or drop correlated duplicates); if the goal is pure prediction, the high VIF in model 4 is tolerable — though a regularised model (Ridge/Lasso) would be the more principled answer.

Report — Strengths, Limitations and Conclusions¶

Summary of what was done¶

Step Decision taken
Preprocessing 19 columns with NA repaired by four documented rules ("None" for absent-feature categoricals, 0 for their numeric counterparts, Neighborhood median for LotFrontage, mode for Electrical); all 1,460 rows retained; no imputation touched the target
Features GrLivArea, OverallQual, YearBuilt, GarageArea; extended with TotalBsmtSF, LotArea, and an interaction term
Validation one 80/20 split (random_state = 42) reused for every model, plus 5-fold CV on the baseline
Best model log(SalePrice) on six features: test R² = 0.8642, RMSE = $32,269, MAE = $20,303

Strengths¶

  1. Strong explanatory power for four variables. R² = 0.77 from GrLivArea, OverallQual, YearBuilt and GarageArea alone — 4 of 79 available predictors — showing how concentrated the price signal is in size and quality.
  2. Fully interpretable. Every coefficient is a price in dollars ($52.97 per ft², $22,708.55 per quality point). A surveyor can audit the model by hand, which no ensemble method allows; the worked example above reproduces model.predict() with a pen-and-paper sum.
  3. No overfitting, and cheap to fit. Test R² ≥ train R², 5 parameters, millisecond training, no hyperparameters to tune. The model is a defensible baseline that any more complex approach must beat.
  4. Honest, reproducible pipeline. A fixed random_state, one split shared by all five specifications, metrics always reported on held-out data, and imputation that never looks at SalePrice.
  5. Diagnostics drove the improvements. The non-linearity found in Step 2 was not left as a remark — it motivated the interaction term and the log target, which together lifted R² from 0.77 to 0.86 and cut typical error by $9,775.

Limitations¶

  1. Linearity is the wrong shape for this market. Price is multiplicative (a quality upgrade is worth proportionally more on a large house), and the quality ladder is convex: +$28k from quality 5→6 versus +$93k from 8→9. A single slope must average these, which is precisely why the interaction and log specifications do better.
  2. Heteroscedastic, skewed residuals. The residual spread grows with the prediction and skews +2.94. OLS's constant-variance assumption is violated, so the usual confidence intervals and p-values on the coefficients would be understated. Any interval reported from this model should be treated as indicative only.
  3. Systematic failure at the top of the market. The top price quartile is under-predicted by $29,665 on average with an RMSE of $70,286 (2.6× the rest), and the single worst miss is $308,144 on a $755,000 home. Luxury value lives in features the model never sees.
  4. Relative error is worst at the bottom. 25.1% MAPE in the cheapest quartile: four positive coefficients give the model no mechanism to predict a genuinely low price, so it pulls the cheapest houses up toward the mean.
  5. No categorical information at all. Neighborhood, KitchenQual, ExterQual, SaleCondition and 39 other text columns are dropped. In real estate, location is the dominant price factor — omitting it is the model's biggest single gap, and it means the coefficients absorb location effects they should not (omitted-variable bias).
  6. Outliers are left in. The two SaleCondition = Partial houses (Id 524 and 1299: 4,676 and 5,642 ft², quality 10, yet sold for $184,750 and $160,000) are high-leverage points that flatten the GrLivArea slope for everyone else. They are incomplete sales, not ordinary market transactions.
  7. Narrow domain of validity. One county (Ames, Iowa), one period (2006–2010, spanning the housing crash), and no inflation adjustment. The coefficients should not be transported to another market or to today's prices.
  8. Single split. The 5-fold CV range (R² 0.53–0.80) shows how much the score depends on which luxury houses land in the test set; the headline 0.7695 is one draw from a fairly wide distribution.

What would improve it next¶

One-hot encode Neighborhood and the quality ordinals (likely the single largest gain available), keep the log target, drop or cap the Partial sales, use Ridge or Lasso so correlated features and interactions can be added without destabilising the coefficients, and report k-fold CV rather than a single split. A gradient-boosted tree on the full 79 columns is the natural next benchmark — but it would give up the clean dollar-per-square-foot interpretation that makes this model worth keeping as a reference.

Consolidated answers to all discussion questions¶

Step Question Answer in brief
1 Columns with missing values? 19 of 81 (7,829 cells, 6.62%); 5 columns >50% missing
1 Strategy and why? Category-aware imputation, not deletion — NA is a documented "feature absent" level; dropna() would leave 0 rows
2 Strongest correlation? OverallQual, r = +0.791 (positive); then GrLivArea 0.709, GarageArea 0.623, YearBuilt 0.523 — all positive
2 Non-linearity? Yes — Spearman > Pearson for all four (YearBuilt +0.130), a convex quality ladder, and variance growing 4.6× with size
3 Regression equation? SalePrice = −845,603.74 + 52.97·GrLivArea + 22,708.55·OverallQual + 395.57·YearBuilt + 57.70·GarageArea
3 Effect of one unit of GrLivArea? +$52.97 per ft² (+$5,297 per 100 ft²; +$27,778 per SD), down from $102/ft² in the simple regression
3 Negative coefficients? None — all four are positive; a negative one would signal a true negative effect, collinearity suppression, or mis-specified form
4 R² and what it indicates? 0.7695 test (train 0.7454; CV 0.7362 ± 0.1027) — 77% of price variance explained, no overfitting, typical miss $26,879
4 Where does it perform poorly? High end in dollars (Q4: −$29,665 bias, RMSE $70,286) and low end in percentage (Q1: 25.1% MAPE); reliable in the $127k–209k middle
5 Do more features help? Yes — R² 0.7695 → 0.7957 (+2 features) → 0.8239 (+interaction) → 0.8642 (log target), with diminishing returns
5 Multicollinearity? Mild in models 1–3 (all VIF < 2.6, max pairwise r = 0.593); severe but artificial with the raw interaction (VIF 30.6), fixed by centring at identical R²
